lead: Every method here starts by classifying the equation. Order counts the highest derivative. Degree is the power of that derivative after clearing fractions and radicals in the derivatives. Linearity asks whether y and its derivatives appear only to power one, multiplied by functions of x. Correct labels choose the method: integrating factor for linear first order, direct integration for separable. Wrong labels break the working.
prereq: You need: first-year calculus — derivatives, the chain rule and basic integrals. Nothing more.

sections.h3: Ordinary or partial, and the order

blocks.text: An equation containing a derivative is a differential equation. One independent variable (x) and one unknown function y gives an ordinary differential equation (ODE). Two or more independent variables with partial derivatives gives a partial differential equation (PDE). Unit 1 covers ODEs; Unit 4 starts PDEs.
The order is the order of the highest derivative present. y′ + xy = 0 has order 1. y″ + 3y′ + 2y = 0 has order 2. (y′)² + y = x has order 1: the square does not raise the order.
Notation: y′ = dy/dx, y″ = d²y/dx², and y⁽ⁿ⁾ = dⁿy/dxⁿ. The order is the largest n that actually appears.
Use: a first-order ODE tracks one quantity against one variable — tea cooling, a UPI wallet earning interest, a capacitor discharging in a power cut.

sections.h3: Degree: read it only after clearing

blocks.text: Degree exists only when the equation is a polynomial in all derivatives. It is then the power of the highest-order derivative.

items: Find the highest-order derivative; that fixes the order.
Clear fractions and radicals in the derivatives.
Read the power of that highest derivative — that is the degree.

blocks.text: Example: (y″)<sup>1/2</sup> = y. Squaring gives y″ = y². The equation is now polynomial in y″, with power 1, so degree is 1, not 1/2. Squaring can add solutions; check the final answer.
(d²y/dx²)³ + x(dy/dx)⁵ = y is polynomial. Order 2, from y″. Degree 3, the power of y″.
Some equations have no degree. sin(y′) = x and e<sup>y′</sup> = x are not polynomial in y′, so the degree is not defined. Say that; do not invent a number.

sections.h3: Linearity: what is allowed in y

blocks.where: y is the unknown function of x; y⁽ᵏ⁾ is its k-th derivative; aₙ(x), …, a₀(x) depend on x only; f(x) is the forcing term.

blocks.text: Allowed: y and every derivative to power one, multiplied only by functions of x, then added. Banned: products such as y·y′, powers above one (y², (y′)³), and nonlinear functions (sin y, e<sup>y</sup>, √y).
Linearity is about y, not x. x²y′ + cos(x)·y = e<sup>x</sup> is linear: x², cos x and e<sup>x</sup> are only coefficients in x.
A first-order ODE can be written in three ways: solved form y′ = f(x, y); differential form M(x, y)dx + N(x, y)dy = 0, used for exact equations; and dy/dx = −M/N, after dividing by N dx.
A first-order linear equation is y′ + P(x)y = Q(x); 1.5 solves it with an integrating factor. Bernoulli's equation 1.6 has this shape but is nonlinear and needs a substitution.

The general solution of an nth-order ODE has exactly n arbitrary constants. Fixing them, usually from a condition such as y(0) = 3, gives a particular solution. Example: y′ = 2x gives y = x² + C; y(0) = 3 forces C = 3, so y = x² + 3.
A family of curves defines an ODE. Take y = ax² + b. Then y′ = 2ax, y″ = 2a. Eliminate a and b: a = y″/2, so y′ = 2·(y″/2)·x, that is x y″ = y′. Two constants gave a second-order ODE.

blocks.where: f(p) is any differentiable function of p. Clairaut's form is first order: y appears only to the first power, while p may appear in any way. If f(p) is a polynomial, the degree is its power (degree 2 for y = px + p²); otherwise degree is not defined.

blocks.text: Method: differentiate with respect to x, using dy/dx = p. Then p = p + x(dp/dx) + f′(p)(dp/dx), so (x + f′(p))(dp/dx) = 0. If dp/dx = 0, p = c and y = cx + f(c) is the general solution. If x + f′(p) = 0, p is a function of x and y gives a singular solution — an extra curve touching every member of the family.

figure.caption: The tree splits by order, then by linearity. y′² and y·y′ are nonlinear even though y′ is only first derivative.

spec.aria: A classification tree splits ordinary differential equations by order first, then by linearity, with a short example at each leaf.

examples.question: Classify each equation by order, degree and linearity: (i) (d²y/dx²)³ + x(dy/dx)⁵ = y; (ii) y′ = y² + x; (iii) y = px + p² where p = dy/dx. Then solve (iii).
steps: (i) Highest derivative d²y/dx² → order 2. Power of d²y/dx² is 3 → degree 3. A derivative has power 3 → nonlinear.
(ii) Highest derivative y′ → order 1, power 1 → degree 1. y² on the right → nonlinear.
(iii) y = xp + p²: order 1. Polynomial in p with highest power 2 → degree 2. p² makes it nonlinear.
(iii) Differentiate, using dy/dx = p and d(p²)/dx = 2p dp/dx: p = p + x dp/dx + 2p dp/dx.
(iii) Branch dp/dx = 0: p = c, so y = cx + c², the general solution.
(iii) Branch x + 2p = 0: p = −x/2, so y = x(−x/2) + x²/4 = −x²/4, the singular solution.
(iii) Check c = 3: y = 3x + 9 equals xp + p² with p = 3. At x = 4, p = −2 gives xp + p² = −4 = −x²/4.
examples.answer: Equation (i) is order 2, degree 3, nonlinear; (ii) is order 1, degree 1, nonlinear; (iii) is order 1, degree 2, nonlinear, with general solution y = cx + c² and singular solution y = −x²/4.
examples.check:
c = 3
print(c)
print(c*c)
x = 4.0
p = -x/2
print(p)
print(-x*x/4)
print(x*p + p*p)

traps: Degree exists only after the equation is polynomial in derivatives. (y″)<sup>1/2</sup> = y squares to y″ = y², so degree is 1, not 1/2. Radicals are a favourite mark-loser.
Linearity is about y and its derivatives, not x. x²y′ + cos(x)·y = 0 is linear; coefficients may be ugly.
Order comes from highest derivative, not highest power. (y′)⁴ + y″ = 0 has order 2, not 4.
y′ = y² has y′ to power one, so students call it linear. It is nonlinear because y has power 2.
In Clairaut's equation, factor out dp/dx; never divide by it. Dividing loses the singular solution y = −x²/4 in y = px + p².

quiz.q: Define the order and the degree of an ODE, and state when the degree exists.
quiz.a: Order is the highest derivative's order. Degree is the power of that highest derivative after the equation becomes polynomial in all derivatives; sin(y′) = x has no degree.

quiz.q: y′ = y² has the derivative y′ to power one. Why is the equation still nonlinear?
quiz.a: Linearity restricts y too. Here y appears as y², power 2, so it cannot be written a₁(x)y′ + a₀(x)y = f(x). It is nonlinear.

quiz.q: Find the order, degree and linearity of (y″)² + (y′)⁵ = x sin y.
quiz.a: Order 2 from y″; degree 2 from (y″)². The (y′)⁵ term and sin y are nonlinear. Answer: order 2, degree 2, nonlinear.

quiz.q: Classify x²y″ + sin(x)·y = 0 by order, degree and linearity.
quiz.a: Order 2, degree 1, linear: it matches a₂(x)y″ + a₀(x)y = f(x) with a₂ = x², a₀ = sin x, f = 0. The sine is of x, not y.

quiz.q: A student claims sin(y′) = x has degree 1 because nothing is raised to a power. Correct the student.
quiz.a: y′ sits inside a sine, so the equation is not polynomial in y′. Degree is undefined. A degree needs polynomial form in the derivatives.

quiz.q: Eliminate the constants a and b from y = a sin x + b cos x and state the order and linearity of the resulting ODE.
quiz.a: y′ = a cos x − b sin x, y″ = −a sin x − b cos x = −y. Hence y″ + y = 0: order 2, degree 1, linear. Two constants give second order.

quiz.q: For y = px + p², why can the curve y = −x²/4 never be obtained from y = cx + c² for any value of c?
quiz.a: Every y = cx + c² is a line; y = −x²/4 is a parabola. Solving cx + c² = −x²/4 gives x² + 4cx + 4c² = 0, i.e. (x + 2c)² = 0: a double root at x = −2c. The line touches once and never coincides, so the parabola is singular.

beyond: Not for the exam. A system of first-order linear ODEs is Y′ = A(x)Y + B(x); eigenvalues of A(x) control behaviour, leading to Unit 2's phase-plane work. y′ = y² shows blow-up: y = 1/(C − x) goes to infinity as x → C. Clairaut's singular solution is an envelope, the same object as a caustic in optics. Search: 'Clairaut equation envelope', 'Lipschitz condition'.
